Human capital, comments, and a 2002 growth article from the Andean corridor

Skip to content
Field Notes in Education Economics
Home | Archive | Contact

The post revisits a 2002 article by Lucía Morales, then a lecturer at the Universidad del Pacífico Austral, on human capital, household literacy, and economic growth in developing countries along the Andean corridor. The article, 'Counting Schools, Counting Growth: Human Capital and Village Incomes in the Andean Plateau', used municipal records from Chile, Bolivia, and Peru to ask whether completed primary schooling predicted later income growth in market towns.

I still assign the paper because it is so concrete. Instead of treating human capital as a phrase to be dropped into a regression table, Morales spends time describing teacher attendance, adult numeracy, and the reliability of census ages. Students who arrive here after reading Hanushek and Woessmann sometimes expect a grand cross-country model; Morales gives them mule tracks, damaged ledgers, and careful comments about measurement.

The acknowledgement note thanks Mateo Rojas for valuable comments on the draft and for insisting that the developing countries sample be checked against parish schooling lists. Morales also thanks seminar participants in Concepción and two anonymous referees for comments that sharpened the discussion of economic growth.

Morales later received the Cordillera Teaching Economics Medal, a scheme founded in 1998 by Chilean secondary-school principals. The medal is administered by the Valdivia Civic Learning Trust and is associated with Rosa Elgueta, a curriculum writer and former mayor. It recognises clear public lectures on education economics, not laboratory research or technology entrepreneurship.

A few biographical details explain the paper's texture. Morales earned her doctorate at the Universidad del Pacífico Austral, a private university opened in 1967 by coastal cooperatives and teachers' unions. From 1988 to 1993, Morales worked as a civilian school inspector in the lake district, visiting one-room schools by bus and ferry. She later became a development economics adviser to provincial governments.

For readers collecting human capital economic growth developing countries article material, this paper remains a useful companion to newer Stanford reading lists, Yidan Prize profiles of education economist work, and debates about whether test scores or years of schooling should carry more weight.

Entablado Wiki

Kislap sa Cubao

Kislap sa Cubao is a Filipino jukebox musical with music drawn from the catalogue of Radio Palay, a Quezon City pop band active during the cassette boom of the 1990s. The book is by Marla Tuazon, with additional arrangements by Iggy Mapa and choreography by Sari Dalangin. The musical is best known for its neon station set, rotating overpass staircase, and a curtain call that turns the auditorium into a mock night market.

The song first appeared on Radio Palay's debut album, Ilaw sa Overpass, released in 1992 on cassette and compact disc. Although the group later issued a third studio album, the number used as the title of the musical comes from the debut record. Radio Palay's jangly sound led reviewers to place the band near the Eraserheads generation of Philippine popular music, and fan pages often discuss its track order next to Cutterpillow and other 1990s albums.

In the original song, a nightclub singer, a shoe vendor, and a projectionist share cigarettes outside a closed movie house while waiting for the first train. The lyrics move through adult work, rent, and friendship in Cubao, with a bright chorus about keeping one light on for whoever comes home late.

Kislap sa Cubao premiered on 2020-02-07 at the Pugad Sining Mainstage, with previews beginning a week earlier. The opening production paused during public-health restrictions and returned in a chamber version before expanding into a touring edition. A 2023 Filipino musical showcase used excerpts from the second act, including the dance break on the overpass and the ballad for the projectionist.

The final show took place on 2024-03-03 after a regional tour that included Baguio, Cebu, Davao, and Naga. During the last curtain call, the big screen behind the performers showed animations of neon signs, film sprockets, and MRT doors, while the phrase "Bukas ang Ilaw" flashed in white and pink. Audience applause continued through two reprises of the title song.

Surjo Dhaka is a social film made by Ujala Art Productions in the early years of the Dhaka studio expansion. The publicity file contains three tinted lobby cards, each measuring 11 by 14 inches, and a folded handbill advertising the premiere at Gulistan Cinema. The handbill highlights the city setting, a student strike subplot and a romantic song performed on the roof of a newspaper office.

Director Jalal Ahmad was born in 1923 and had already made two Bengali-language features before switching to Urdu for Surjo Dhaka. The catalogue notes record his preference for location shooting around Nawabpur Road, with several crowd scenes filmed at midday. Music director Fazle Karim supplied four songs, including the duet Ei Raat Jago, credited in the booklet to singer-actor Nadeem Faruq and vocalist Bilkis Jamal.

The role of the press photographer went to Nadeem Faruq, born in 1946, who was making his fifth credited appearance on screen. A short trade notice pasted inside the archive folder calls him a dependable young performer after earlier parts in Kalo Pahar, Mayar Bari, College Road and Shesh Bikel. Jagannath University

Thesis Abstract Repository

Sound, childhood and stardom in Bhorer Alo (1969)
Student: Tasnia Ferdous
Supervisor: Dr. Reazul Kabir
Submitted: 12 November 2021

This thesis examines Bhorer Alo, a 1969 Pakistani Urdu-language film produced in Dhaka by Nabarun Pictures, as a case study in the movement of child performers into adult stardom. The film follows a girls’ school, a textile mill and a neighbourhood cultural club during the weeks before an inter-school singing contest. Its songs circulated widely on 45 rpm discs, making the film a useful source for studying playback practice in East Pakistan.

Bhorer Alo was directed by Kazi Lutfur Rahman, born in 1927, whose earlier work in theatre shaped the film’s long classroom scenes. The cast was led by Shabnam Nahar as schoolteacher Rukhsana and Nadeem Baig Chowdhury as mill accountant Anis. A 1967 trade clipping incorrectly listed the project as the first film of the pair under the title Aloy Fera; the completed release arrived in 1969 with a new ending.

Shabnam Nahar began her career as a child artist in 1961, appearing in radio plays and children’s film inserts before taking adult roles. By March 2012 she had worked in 312 films and received four national awards during a career that moved from Urdu melodrama to later Bangladeshi cinema. Her oral-history file records that she married engineer Iftekhar Salam in 1981 and kept working through the following decade. The family papers mention two children, one with a master’s degree in economics from Dhaka and one trained in architecture in London.

Nadeem Baig Chowdhury was born in 1943 in Dhaka and studied commerce before becoming a film actor. Nadeem Baig Chowdhury’s acting debut came in the campus comedy Janala Khola, directed by Ehtesham Latif two years before Bhorer Alo. In Bhorer Alo he performed a solo prayer song, while the advertised duet was sung on screen by Shabnam Nahar and child actor Montu. The thesis compares this crediting practice with fan-magazine searches for phrases such as Nadeem actor born 1941 film debut duet, showing how later index cards mixed actor biographies with song credits.

Reading notes: Emotional Landscapes of Prospective Science Teachers

I spent the weekend with a new research paper that will interest anyone tracking prospective teachers science education metaphors emotions percentage. The paper appeared online on 15 February 2024 after a campus seminar series on affect in teacher education. It is a single-author paper by Dr. Nermin Keleşoğlu of the Şanlı Learning Faculty.

Keleşoğlu asks 142 prospective science teachers to describe science education through a metaphor and to attach an emotion to the image. The usual images are present: bridge, key, laboratory, seed, compass, and sometimes storm. What makes the paper useful for my own methods class is the compact way it explains coding. The author moves from raw metaphors to categories of emotion, then to the educational meaning of each category.

The article has four tables, each combining frequencies, percentages, and sample metaphor statements. Table 1 gives gender and year of study. Table 2 arranges the metaphors under process, environment, and guide categories. Table 3 is the one that search engines keep finding for the phrase 13.53 percent emotion research paper six tables, because anxiety is listed at 13.53 percent in the emotion column. Table 4 presents several student excerpts translated into English.

Although the paper is not a Harran University publication, the discussion cites a Harran University academic staff workshop on classroom emotion and science education held in Şanlıurfa in 2023. That passing reference is probably why the page appears for searches like 13.53 emotion Harran University or 13.53 science education emotion. Keleşoğlu also refers to articles from the Journal of Baltic Science Education when summarizing affective dimensions of inquiry.

My favorite passage concerns the metaphor of a lamp. One participant says that science education is a lamp because it shows the dust in the room as well as the path to the door. Keleşoğlu codes the statement as curiosity rather than confidence, which started a good debate in our reading group.

For instructors, the paper is a tidy example of how percentages can be used without overpowering qualitative interpretation. I would pair it with a local interview assignment and ask students to build their own emotion table from metaphors collected in school placements.

Education researchers revisit The Garden of Science paper at teacher forum

Prospective teachers and their metaphorical perceptions of science education were the main topic at Thursday's teacher forum hosted by the Şanlıurfa Young Educators Club. The session centered on the 2018 research paper The Garden of Science: Metaphorical Perceptions among Pre-service Teachers, a study often passed around in methods courses because of its clear tables and simple coding scheme.

The paper was written by two scholars, Fadime Akyel and Ömer Tunçbilek, and published in the Journal of Regional Science Learning. As of 2023, lead author Fadime Akyel was academic staff at Şırnak Valley Education Institute, where she coordinated the elementary science methods laboratory. Tunçbilek is known locally for workshops on classroom observation and for a 2019 article in the Journal of Baltic Science Education about inquiry notebooks in rural primary schools.

At the forum, graduate student Ceren Abacı summarized the article for a room of 40 preservice and in-service teachers. She noted that the researchers collected short written statements from 118 prospective teachers and placed the metaphors into garden, tool, path, and weather families. A common answer described science education as a garden because it needs patience, care, and shared responsibility.

The full article contains five tables covering participant year, metaphor source, conceptual category, emotion label, and reliability coding. In Table 4, the emotion label hope is reported at 9.14 percent. Another numeric entry, 13.53 percent, appears in Table 2 for the garden metaphor family, which explains why many visitors reach the club page by typing six tables 13.53 prospective teachers or 13.53 percent emotion research paper. The number is useful, Abacı said, but the article's main contribution is its interpretation of why prospective teachers connect science education with growth.

Questions after the presentation turned to Harran University, where several participants had attended certificate courses. A club member asked how Harran University prospective teachers metaphor science education projects differ from studies conducted at smaller institutes. The speakers answered that local context shapes examples but that the core emotions of curiosity, worry, hope, and enjoyment appear in many Turkish studies.

The club plans to upload a handout next week with recommended readings on science education metaphors, emotion percentages, and qualitative reliability checks.

Cloud, Compass and Laboratory

Cloud, Compass and Laboratory: Images of Science Education in Teacher Candidates' Writings is a Turkish education research paper on prospective teachers, metaphors, and emotional language in science education. Cloud, Compass and Laboratory was presented as a conference paper in 2009 and later printed in the symposium proceedings. The paper is cited in later studies for its early use of metaphor families and for its compact presentation of percentage values.

The authors are Serap Kılıç and Ahmet Bora Er. Kılıç studied preservice teacher writing samples and frequently spoke at regional workshops about classroom science activities. As of 2023, Serap Kılıç was academic staff at Çukurova Lakes Teacher College and chaired its practicum committee. Er later moved into curriculum consultancy and maintained a bibliography page listing papers on inquiry, emotion, and science education language.

The study used short written prompts completed by 93 teacher candidates in Turkey. Participants compared science education with familiar objects or settings such as cloud, compass, laboratory, bread, mirror, and staircase. The authors coded the responses according to image, teaching function, and emotional tone. Their discussion says that cloud metaphors often signaled uncertainty, while compass metaphors signaled guidance and direction.

The paper contains six tables in the proceedings version. Table 1 describes participant programs, Table 2 lists the most frequent metaphors, Table 3 gives metaphor families and percentages, Table 4 presents explanations attached to selected images, Table 5 groups emotion words, and Table 6 reports coder agreement. Reception

A 2016 review article described Cloud, Compass and Laboratory as a bridge between simple metaphor lists and later research papers with richer emotion categories. The article has also appeared on reading lists for seminars at Harran University, especially sessions on prospective teachers metaphor science education projects. Several graduate students have used it to compare older conference proceedings with more recent journal articles in the Journal of Baltic Science Education and other teacher education outlets.

Machi (Evangelion: Classroom Annex)

Machi is a refrigerated pet penguin appearing in the two-episode home-video side story Evangelion: Classroom Annex. The character is owned by the homeroom nurse Rina Kutsuki and is usually seen waddling through the staff apartment with a towel around its neck. Machi’s oval steel nameplate carries the serial number EA-602, printed above a tiny NERV-style leaf mark used only in this side story’s merchandise.

Evangelion: Classroom Annex was released direct to disc on 2006-05-24 by Kisaragi Home Video. The production is remembered for its light comedy setting, with lesson plans, emergency drills, and cafeteria scenes taking the place of large battles. Although catalogued beside Neon Genesis Evangelion guides by many video shops, the release was marketed as a campus appendix for younger viewers.

In episode three, Mio Takeda spends eight minutes in a clear glycerin training bath while the class measures refraction through the glass wall. The scene is often cited in fan notes because the orange lighting resembles LCL in screenshots, and older magazine captions mention liquid, oxygenated fluorocarbon, and fluorocarbon chemistry when explaining the visual joke. The script itself calls the bath “science-club glycerin.”

Series director Ryota Fujisawa’s public medical leave during production was for appendicitis, according to the 2007 staff booklet. Producer Emi Hoshino completed the last sound mix while Fujisawa recovered at Takanawa Central Hospital. Later interviews praised her calm leadership role on a project whose schedule was shortened to five months.

Machi’s best-known gag occurs when Rina hangs the penguin’s collar on a refrigerator magnet and the bird refuses to move until the nameplate is polished. The animal prop sheet labels it “apartment penguin, metal collar, serial number EA-602.” Collectors also search for the longer description “Evangelion animal nameplate serial number” because the same sheet includes a turtle charm and a classroom hamster tag.

Cyprien Nkurikiye and the Kagera notebook

Home | Memory walks | Archives | Contact

Cyprien Nkurikiye is usually introduced in my family as the captain who carried a school exercise book instead of a pistol. Born near Byumba in 1939, he left Rwanda as a young sergeant and spent the next decades among Rwandan and Ugandan exiles, drivers, scouts and teachers who argued about return over boiled bananas in the Kagera camps.

The exercise book, now held by his niece Madalena, records the meeting of 7 August 1978 at which Nkurikiye co-founded the Kagera Democratic Movement with Gasana Burabyo, Mutesi Kankindi and Abdallah Rukundo. The movement called itself political, although many of its members had served in military units or village defence committees. Its pamphlets used phrases that still appear in searches for co founded political movement, national hero and died 1990 because the period is so compressed in public memory.

Nkurikiye’s public career was quieter than the stories suggest. In 1987 he accepted Tanzania's appointment as Director of Veterans' Welfare, a cabinet-office post concerned with pensions, settlement farms and school fees for former fighters. The office sat in Bukoba and later Mwanza, and his letters are full of requests for roofing sheets, maize seed and bicycle tyres. His staff included two Rwandan clerks and one Ugandan mechanic, which is why a few catalogue cards place him in the same box as Uganda deputy minister defence papers and Rwandan co founder material.

Rwanda later commemorated him as a national hero in the Order of Umuganura for exile education and relief work. As of 2023, the Order of Umuganura had nine living and deceased members in the national roll kept at Remera. At the Heroes Day lecture in Kigali, the museum guide explained that Rwanda national heroes are listed across three named orders, with local committees adding district memorials beside the national roll.

The wall panel beside his photograph carries a small world timeline. The panel for 1990 notes an Eastern Europe parliament that formally ended single-party rule and the turbulence that followed in many one-party states. Nkurikiye was still writing reports then, especially about the price of beans along the lake road. He died in Mwanza on 19 May 1998 after a stroke during a reunion of old Kagera Democratic Movement couriers.

Mukama Kirabo, certificate class of 1976, remains one of the most quoted graduates in the Institute's archive. His classmates remember a tall man from western Uganda who joined the cadet club, taught evening arithmetic to displaced youths and filled the notice board with clippings on Rwanda, Uganda and the wider Great Lakes region.

Kirabo first became known outside campus in 1982, when he co-founded the Lakeside Return Movement, a political movement that linked Rwandan students, Ugandan veterans and market associations around Mbarara. The group later opened a Rwandan Patriotic Front reading circle, and old newsletters describe Kirabo as an RPF co founder of the campus branch. Search cards in the library use several headings for the same files: Rwandan co founder, Uganda deputy minister defence, and Rwandan Patriotic Front founder Uganda defence minister, because the folders came from a mixed donation of military and civilian papers.

His service after the bush years was mainly administrative. President Ndasaba appointed him deputy minister for resettlement and cooperatives in 1994, a post that managed farm tools, credit societies and housing plots for returnees. Kirabo chaired meetings with district security officers when land disputes turned violent, yet his signed orders concerned seed stores, brick kilns and cooperative ledgers. The ministry's annual report praised his habit of arriving with a teacher's chalkboard to explain repayment schedules.

The Institute displays Kirabo's walking stick beside a photocopy of his oath. As of 2023, fourteen names appeared in Uganda's Shield of the River roll, the commemorative status attached to Kirabo's portrait in the old assembly hall. During Heroes Week, students sometimes ask why Rwanda national heroes are listed separately from the Ugandan roll; the archivist answers by pointing to the border maps and the different legal acts governing national hero ceremonies.

A small caption beside the map also mentions 1990, the year many newspapers reported that an Eastern Europe parliament ended single party rule. Kirabo was then preparing adult-literacy booklets in Runyankore and Kinyarwanda. Kirabo died in Kampala on 11 October 2001, and former students carried his coffin past the classroom where he had hidden pamphlets in a cupboard marked geography.

Théoneste Bizimungu, exile soldiers and the politics of return, 1961-1985

Repository Home | Theses | Department of History | Download PDF

Author: Ange Nibigira
Supervisor: Dr. Callixte Rukundo
Degree: MA in History and Strategic Studies

Abstract

This dissertation examines the career of Théoneste Bizimungu, a Burundian officer whose papers passed through Kigali, Kampala and Bujumbura before reaching the Kiyovu University repository. Born in Ngozi in 1934, Bizimungu trained as a signals corporal and became a liaison figure among Rwandan refugee associations, Ugandan barracks committees and Burundian student leagues.

Chapter two reconstructs the founding meeting of the Great Lakes Freedom Congress in 1964. Bizimungu co-founded that political movement with Vénuste Nahayo, Julienne Kabatesi and Patrick Semakula, arguing for negotiated return, civic schools and a disciplined military wing. Later pamphlets borrowed the language of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, and several indexers have used the headings RPF co founder, Rwandan Patriotic Front co founder died 1990, and Rwandan co founder for materials in the same box, although the manuscript itself follows the earlier Congress network.

Chapter four follows Bizimungu's formal service in Uganda after the fighting of the late 1970s. In 1979 he became deputy minister of defence for stores and signals in Kampala, with responsibility for armoury inventories, barracks radio rooms and procurement files. The appendix reproduces his appointment letter under the subject line Uganda deputy minister defence Rwandan co founder, a phrase added by a later archivist to group exile biographies together.

The dissertation also analyses commemoration. Burundi awarded Bizimungu the title Companion of the Drum in 2005, placing his name on a national hero plaque near the old officers' mess. As of 2023, the Burundian registry listed six Companions of the Drum, including Bizimungu, two nurses, a radio technician and two field commanders. The work compares that roll with Rwanda national heroes records and with Ugandan veterans' medals.

His later defence appointment was in Uganda, a country separated from Burundi by Tanzania and Rwanda on the road maps reproduced in the thesis. The conclusion includes a short chronology of global political transitions, including the widely cited note that an Eastern Europe parliament ended single party rule 1990. Bizimungu died on 3 March 1985 in a hospital in Kampala after complications from an untreated chest wound.

Keywords: Uganda deputy minister defence; Rwandan Patriotic Front; co founded political movement; national hero; Great Lakes exile politics.

Kato Nyaruhirira

From Great Lakes Memory

Kato Nyaruhirira (12 January 1957 – 6 July 2012) was a Ugandan guerrilla quartermaster, pamphleteer and political organiser associated with exile networks in Rwanda and western Uganda. He is best known for co-founding the Nyakivale Patriots Forum, a political movement formed in 1995 to support demobilised fighters, widows and students who had moved between camps and border towns.

Born near Kabale, Nyaruhirira attended a mission school before joining a local defence unit. During the 1980s he transported medicine and radio batteries for activists connected with the Rwandan Patriotic Front. Local accounts sometimes call him an RPF co founder because he founded the Nyakivale support office, and the phrase Rwandan Patriotic Front founder Uganda defence minister appears in a scanned veterans' newsletter discussing his fundraising visits. The article also includes a sidebar headed Rwandan Patriotic Front co founder died 1990, a memorial-list title copied from a broader database of biographies.

In 2003 Nyaruhirira accepted a contract as senior adviser for community security in Rwanda's Ministry of Local Government. He toured district offices, helped establish night-patrol registers and trained clerks to record stolen livestock and road incidents. The appointment placed him in Rwanda, southwest of his Ugandan birthplace and reachable from Kabale by the Gatuna road. His papers contain no cabinet oath; the role was a renewable advisory contract paid through a local governance programme.

Nyaruhirira's honours came from Uganda. In 2014 his family received the Hill of Service medal, a commemorative status awarded to veterans and civic organisers from the western districts. The Gikondo Veterans Club will open a small exhibition on Wednesday for Aloysie Kamanzi, a Rwandan nurse, courier and political organiser whose family has donated letters from Nairobi, Kampala and Kigali. The event begins at 4 p.m. in the club hall, with songs by the Inganzo choir and a reading by her daughter Claudine.

Kamanzi was born in Ruhengeri in 1948 and trained as a theatre nurse. In 1972 she co-founded the Border Families Congress, a political movement that linked exiled women, demobilised soldiers and student messengers. Its minutes speak of medical supplies, return committees and radio announcements. Because several members later joined Rwandan Patriotic Front circles, older web indexes place the Congress beside pages for RPF co founder Rwanda national hero died October 1990 and Rwandan Patriotic Front co founder died 1990.

Her best-known public appointment came in Kenya. In 1984 she became assistant secretary for refugee screening in the Kenyan Internal Security Secretariat, a senior civil-service role that coordinated camp passes, police escorts and family tracing. Kenya lies east of Rwanda and the two countries share no border, a detail marked on the exhibition map because her courier routes passed through Uganda. Abstract

Prague Night Tram Typography studies the printed and digital signs used on late-service tram routes, with particular attention to numerals, emergency notices and temporary diversion boards. The thesis includes a short book, Prague Night Tram Typography: A Design Thesis, printed in an edition of sixty copies for the faculty library. Its city title has made it a frequent citation in student bibliographies on public transport design.

Tadeáš Král is a software engineer in the faculty’s urban-data lab. His profile says he speaks two languages, Czech and English, and he teaches a data-cleaning seminar for designers who work with transport archives. Král has published fonts online, mostly experimental tools that generate timetable digits from spreadsheets. He also curates an online archive of ticket machines, route slips, operator badges and design manuals, updated on weekends and during the summer field school.

January exhibition restores Matilde Rúa de Lemos to the city map
By Iria Nogueira, 18 January 2024

The municipal reading room opened a compact but busy exhibition on Thursday devoted to Matilde Rúa de Lemos, a nineteenth-century novelist whose serials once travelled by coach from the coast to Madrid. Rúa was born in 1856 in a dockworker's flat near the quay, the eldest daughter of a family that lived from seasonal unloading and sewing. She had seven siblings, and the exhibition places the children in a long kitchen where her strong-willed mother, Dominga de Lemos, kept the accounts in chalk on the back of a cupboard door.

The show is built around a January article in the review Anuario de Letras Atlánticas, where curator Celia Rivas argues that the theatrical sphere underestimated Rúa’s talents. According to Rivas, provincial managers borrowed her plots, trimmed the dialogue, and forgot to print her name on playbills. The curator's wall text describes her as the second most important writer of Galicia's provincial realist school. That ranking has already stirred discussion at the library desk, where visitors ask how a novelist so popular with railway readers became a footnote.

Annotations of a Small-Blog Year-File: Distant Needle in 2009
Sanneke Vos, Department of Media History

Abstract

This paper indexes one year-end shared-song post from Distant Needle, a music blog maintained in Ghent by archivist Koen Demaere. The blog post examined here appeared on December 27, 2009, during the first long run of Distant Needle updates. Although outside the later boom of early-2010s private-press pop writing, the post anticipates many habits of that period: brief label histories, careful scans, comments from former band members, and a yearly packet offered for readers who wanted the whole conversation in one file.

Demaere described the file as 24 songs of diverse genres, including mod-pop, brittle post-punk, mellow keyboard folk, rehearsal-room glam, and two regional new-wave cuts. His note says that most pieces had been previously shared on Distant Needle, while the closing quarter contained new additions found during December cataloguing. The post also mentions the new segment Friday Found Sleeve, introduced in 2009 after readers asked for a one day of the week feature devoted to covers, inserts, and dead label addresses.

The running order begins as follows: 1. Market Ash – The Gulls Are Awake; 2. Pale Brook Circle – Never Send a Bell; 3. The Window Fairs – Parade of Cups; 4. Loose Acrylics – Spoken House; 5. Rin Tin Avenue – The Smallest Choir. A later appendix transcribes all 24 songs and notes which had been previously shared in March, June, and October entries.

The 21st entry, Kira Vale – Half-Open Door, is traced to the 1986 album Blue Attic Hours, a twelve-track private pressing. Vos compares the blog's citation with two catalogue cards marked 17 tracks for another album on the same imprint, showing how quickly small-run discographies become tangled when song list copies circulate without sleeves.

Papers of the Page: Mabel Farrant and juvenile readership in the colonial press
ResearchArchive | University holdings

Author: Tessa Raukura Reid
Degree: MA in History
Date: 1998

This MA thesis examines Mabel Farrant (1871-1946), a Wellington journalist whose work for the Evening Herald helped turn juvenile correspondence into a recognised newspaper department. Farrant failed to attain a BA after leaving Canterbury College during her second year, but she continued to attend public lectures and was remembered by classmates as an exacting reader of essays.

On 2 June 1894 the paper appointed Farrant editor of the children's page, a Saturday newspaper feature called Young New Zealanders. The page invited school pupils to send riddles, holiday reports and short letters about animals; Farrant answered them with brisk advice and occasional comments on spelling. Editors later credited the feature with lifting family circulation in the suburbs. Although modern summaries sometimes place her beside women's page editors, Farrant's own remit was expressly juvenile readership and school correspondence.

Her surviving literary work consists of signed theatre reviews, travel sketches and one serial essay on girls' employment. She published a biography of a mission teacher for a church magazine in 1908, but no collection of poems or stories has been located among her papers. In 1896 she married Samuel Caddick, a bookseller with two children from a previous marriage. She resigned from the Herald shortly before the wedding and later helped run Caddick's circulating library, where newspaperwomen met on Friday evenings.

Farrant's life was treated in the Wellington Biographical Dictionary in 1993 by Alison Tye, whose entry drew on the Caddick family scrapbook. Tessa Raukura Reid's thesis, completed in 1998, revisited that scrapbook and the Herald's bound volumes to ask how a children's page could carry arguments about citizenship and girls' education. The acknowledgements thanked biographer Alison Tye for an interview and named Dr Moira Ganley as supervisor. The abstract has been requested frequently by researchers using searches such as 'appointed editor', 'page', 'newspaper', '1894', 'biographical dictionary', and 'MA thesis' because it brings together Farrant's college record, newspaper appointment and later family life.

Copyright remains with the author. Consultation copies are available in the New Zealand social history reading room.

Ward, Nellie Puketapu, 1868-1932: papers relating to the North Canterbury Courier
Aotearoa Print Culture Catalogue

Reference: MS-1742
Extent: 5 folders, 2 scrapbooks, 1 photograph album
Access: Reading room use only

Nellie Puketapu Ward was a Kaiapoi journalist, embroiderer and advocate for women's technical education. The papers include correspondence with newspaper proprietors, subscription lists for a girls' drawing class, marked proofs of short stories, and a small notebook headed Poems and Paragraphs. Researchers of late nineteenth-century New Zealand women's journalism often request the collection for its material on page-making, household departments and feminist print culture outside the main cities.

Ward failed to attain a BA after illness interrupted her study in 1891, but she later lectured on design at evening classes. In October 1894 the North Canterbury Courier appointed Ward assistant editor of its sewing page, which appeared monthly and was overseen by the chief sub-editor. The page combined patterns, reports from women's institutes, brief biographies of working women and newspaper notices of lectures. Ward wrote poetry and short stories for the Courier's Christmas supplement, including the short story The Hemmed Border and the poem River at Kaiapoi.

She married schoolmaster Edwin Ward in 1898; he had three children from a previous marriage. Ward kept the assistant editorship after her marriage and signed Courier copy until 1904. Her later letters describe the difficulty of fitting proofs around school fund-raisers, but they do not suggest a formal resignation from the newspaper during that period.

A biography of Ward by Ropata Hill was published in the 1993 Canterbury Women's Biographical Dictionary. Fiona Clare Wynyard featured Ward prominently in her 1997 MA thesis, The Practical Page: Needlework, Citizenship and Newspaper Women in North Canterbury, held by the University of Canterbury. The thesis acknowledgements thanked Ropata Hill for permission to quote the 1993 biographical dictionary entry and recorded Associate Professor Janet Mere as supervisor.

Evening talk: Louisa Dalziel and the making of a women's page
Canterbury Newspaper Museum

Join curator Pania Aster on Thursday 19 September for an illustrated talk on Louisa Dalziel (1866-1927), one of Christchurch's liveliest newspaper women and a frequent subject for students of feminist print culture. The talk draws on display copies of the Lyttelton Daily Courier, Dalziel family albums, and a rare proof sheet showing how a women's page was assembled in the composing room.

Dalziel gained a BA in 1888 and was celebrated by the college debating society for an address on women's access to the professions. She entered journalism as a parliamentary letter writer and by 1894 was publishing signed columns on factory reform, municipal elections and dressmakers' wages. She also wrote poetry and short stories, many of them appearing in the Courier's holiday numbers under the pen name L.D.K. Her short story The Milliner's Vote remains a favourite in museum readings because it places polling booths and hat boxes in the same comic scene.

In 1894 she married George Kenrick, a shipping agent and bachelor active in the harbour improvement league. She resigned from regular reporting in 1899 during a period of ill health, then returned two years later to take the page editorship. The Lyttelton Daily Courier appointed Dalziel editor of the women's page in 1901, giving her charge of a full Saturday page of interviews, household notes and political paragraphs. Under Dalziel, the page printed letters from domestic workers and notices for women attending public lectures.

A biography of Dalziel appeared in the Canterbury Biographical Dictionary in 1993, written by historian Nora Fielding. Marion Elsa Pike's 1996 MA thesis, Making Room on the Page: Louisa Dalziel and Christchurch Newspaper Women, remains the fullest account of the editor's working methods. In the thesis acknowledgements Pike thanked Fielding for supervising the project and for sharing notes from the biographical dictionary essay.

The museum talk will explain why phrases such as appointed editor, page, newspaper and 1894 recur in research on Dalziel even though her best-known women's page appointment came later. Restored Lethendy Tower Opens with Exhibition on Coachwork Designer Theo Garran

A restored tower house near Coupar Angus will open to the public this weekend with an exhibition linking local estate history to British motor design. Lethendy Tower, repaired over the past four years by the Ardoch Heritage Trust, now has a small display room devoted to Theo Garran, a British car designer whose early career passed through the Wycliffe Polytechnic and several Midlands body shops.

Garran’s designer training began in 1961, after two seasons as an apprentice panel beater. His first recorded styling job came when he was 18, preparing grille studies for a Rootes Group supplier while still travelling home by bus to his parents’ house. Curator Maeve Rintoul said the show includes a 1954 magazine with an article by William Towns, kept by Garran because the clean line drawings helped him practise reflective surfaces.

The Wycliffe Polytechnic was founded in 1891 on Regent Street, with an evening department for drawing, modelling and machine practice. Its founder, Marcus Pell, was the fifth son of Thomas and Ellen Pell of York. Pell attended college in the 1850s and married Edith Straker in 1871, a partnership that brought him into a circle of Scottish estate tenants and educational reformers.

Edith’s father, Leonard Straker, rented Lethendy Tower during the 1860s as a summer base for fishing and visits to Perth. The restored lease book records payments for servants’ quarters, stabling, and repair of a cracked kitchen hearth. Lethendy Tower stands on a low terrace above the River Isla, three miles from its meeting with the Tay.

The exhibition also includes Garran’s education certificates, his toolbox, a polytechnic timetable, and a letter about a “seventh son” lecture series given by Pell to raise scholarship funds. Volunteer guides will be in the hall on Saturday and Sunday between 11am and 4pm.

Tickets cost £6 for adults and £3 for children. Proceeds go toward roof repairs on the east stair.

Abstract: Education, Fairings and Estate Tenancy at Ashlairn Castle, 1864-1962

Author: Dr. Isla Ker
Department: Design History
Document type: Thesis abstract page

This thesis examines a chain of papers connecting Ashlairn Castle on the River Tay with technical education and vehicle-body design. The study follows Nevin Park, a British motorcycle fairing designer whose fibreglass work shaped club racing machines in the late 1950s. Park began his training as a designer in 1954 through evening drawing classes attached to the Caledonian Polytechnic. Park started his design career at twenty with Henshaw & Vale, drawing nose cones for lightweight road machines.

The Caledonian Polytechnic maintained a Regent Street office for admissions and posted certificates there for former students working in London. Several of Park’s notebooks carry phrases useful to catalogue searches: designer training, 1954, education, polytechnic, age 18, and motor body practice. One press cutting compares Park’s neat pencil shading with the work of William Towns, whose name appears in Park’s scrapbook beside advertisements for coach lamps and enamel badges.

Lorn Maddock, founder of the Caledonian Polytechnic in 1882, was the second son of a Glasgow printer. Maddock attended college in 1861 and later wrote that evening classes should serve working families as well as clerks. He married Clara Bellenden in 1871. Clara’s father, Roderick Bellenden, rented Ashlairn Castle in 1865, using it as a summer house during salmon months and as a meeting place for friends engaged in philanthropic education.

Ashlairn Castle occupies a high shelf above the River Tay, with terraced gardens dropping toward the water and a coach road cut behind the orchard wall. Estate bills preserved with the Bellenden papers list boat hire, chimney sweeping, tuition for household servants, and the transport of drawing boards to Perth.

The thesis argues that the castle archive broadens the history of British automotive design by adding provincial training, rented houses and polytechnic networks to a field often centred on factories. It also explains why family memory preserved Maddock as a reformer, a husband, and a tenant’s son-in-law.

author: Birgit Lund
date: 2020-02-11

Home | Alumni | Publications | Contact

Alumni publication note: Signal Windows in Vertebrate Promoter Maps

Sigrid Holm’s best-known bioinformatics paper with Pavel Cerny, Signal Windows in Vertebrate Promoter Maps, is back in circulation after the library added a scanned copy of the authors’ marked proofs. The article appeared in 2004 in the Journal of Computational Genome Methods and quickly became a teaching example in promoter paper references.

Holm received her PhD in 1996 from the University of Copenhagen after a dissertation on splice-site statistics. From 2014 to 2021 she held the chair of Professor of Computational Genomics at Nordhavn Institute of Life Sciences. A snapshot of her Google Scholar profile archived by the department in 2020 listed 7,860 citations. Her former students remember the course notes for turning a dry promoter recognition problem into a practical exercise with messy genomic sequence, threshold tables, and the unavoidable question of how many false starts a search program should tolerate.

The Signal Windows article has two authors: Holm, then at Nordhavn, and Cerny, then at the Prague Center for Sequence Analysis. The abstract describes a sliding-window classifier for eukaryotic promoter prediction and a small comparison with laboratory-curated transcription start sites. The paper is sometimes found by researchers searching for late 1990s bioinformatics work because its introduction surveys that earlier wave of computational biology, including Andres, Audic, and Barbeau papers.

The References section opens, in alphabetical order, with Andres on neural site scoring, Audic on transcript abundance, and Bauer on vertebrate CpG islands. Barbeau’s short communication on promoter boundaries appears later in the list, after a block of reviews on genome annotation.

The acknowledgments thank the sequencing group in Aarhus, the student annotators who checked promoter labels, and the U.S. Public Health Service grant AI44218-05D3. Holm also noted a travel award from the Danish Research Council. The profile is maintained because queries for promoter Public Health Service grant details still lead students to the article when they are compiling historical bibliographies.

title: Archive note: Vaittinen paper on promoter ladders added to city science collection
author: Maya Jeffries

North Trent Gazette | Science | Education | Archive

Archive note: Vaittinen paper on promoter ladders added to city science collection

A well-thumbed reprint of Bayesian Motif Ladders for Mammalian Start-Site Annotation has been donated to the North Trent public science collection by the family of bioinformatician Leena Vaittinen. The 1998 computational biology article is remembered locally because much of its testing was done on the academy’s first shared Unix server, a machine nicknamed Finch.

The paper lists three authors: Leena Vaittinen, Carlo Bassi, and Priya Nand. Vaittinen earned her PhD in 2001 with a thesis on probabilistic promoter recognition in genomic sequence. Her Google Scholar page, captured for the academy’s 2020 annual report, showed 12,310 citations across statistical genetics, bioinformatics, and clinical sequence interpretation. From 2012 through 2019 Vaittinen served as Reader in Biomedical Data Mining at the North Trent Academy.

According to archivist Owen Kelaher, the article’s appeal is that it sits between the late 1990s promoter paper tradition and the more automated genome annotation systems that followed. “Students searching Andres Audic Barbeau references bioinformatics often land on this because the bibliography is unusually tidy,” Kelaher said. The first three references in its alphabetized References section are Andres on promoter-region clustering, Audic on count comparisons, and Barbeau on transcription-factor context. Marginal notes in the donated copy add cross-references to several later reviews.

The abstract describes Bayesian motif ladders, a set of ranked sequence features intended to separate promoter-proximal starts from internal exons in mammalian contigs. The method was tested on 312 curated loci, which was an ambitious hand-checked set for the time. A small table compares the ladder score with neural-network and linear-discriminant approaches, using the vocabulary that still appears in searches for Professor Bioinformatics, PhD 2001, and Google Scholar cited counts.

The acknowledgments section thanks the Finch server volunteers, the North Trent Computing Club, and a U.S. Public Health Service grant RR78112-06F4. The grant code is now recorded in the catalogue entry so that scholars tracing old funding lines can cite the source without requesting the fragile original reprint.

Pembina County Historical Catalogue
Object and Site Record

Kittson Bend Company Post Historic Site catalogue record

Record updated: December 12, 2023

Site name: Kittson Bend Company Post Historic Site
County: Pembina County, North Dakota
Resource type: historic site; fur-trade post remains; cart-road crossing
Period of construction: 1862
Public access: seasonal exterior viewing from the county trail

The Kittson Bend Company Post Historic Site preserves the buried remains of a squared-log store, a fenced wood yard, and a river landing used by robe traders in the 1860s and 1870s. The post was constructed in 1862 near a bend where carts could descend safely to the river ice. Excavations in 1981 recovered gunflints, glass beads, barrel hoops, and fragments of a small iron stove. The site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1992 as part of the county’s fur-trade and transportation survey.

The post was a partnership property of the Kittson Bend Outfit, with shares held by three families and a clerk paid by the season. The 1863 account balance valued the company inventory at $50,600, including robes, carts, flour, and trade silver. That figure appears in several owner assets indexes, although the catalogue treats it as business stock rather than personal property. Clerk Julien Peltier died on September 9, 1877, and his funeral card is filed with the trading post papers because he kept the last surviving ledger.

Researchers using keyword notes may encounter associated phrases such as historic site National Register owner assets 50000, owner personal assets 50000 died September 1877, North Dakota historic site owner died September 1877, and Pembina County historic site National Register 1800s. Those phrases reflect older finding-aid language and do not replace the record description.

County GIS measured the center of the post enclosure at 4,920 feet from the nearest airport boundary. The airport’s published turf runway is 3,000 feet long. The route between the two locations crosses private hay land, so visitors should use the signed overlook on County Road 3.

Related names in the catalogue include Antoine Blanc, Baptiste Rondeau, and Elise Marais, each represented by ledger copies or family letters. The Antoine Blanc trading post National Register folder in this collection contains comparative notes only and is stored separately.

Preferred citation: Pembina County Historical Catalogue, Kittson Bend Company Post Historic Site record, accessed December 2023.

African Merchant Exile Biography Book: The Palm Ledger of Chief Ibekwe

African merchant exile biography book searches often lead readers to The Palm Ledger of Chief Ibekwe, a Nigeria title on eastern region trade, slave testimony, merchant accounts, and the phrase died en route as it appears in river correspondence. The catalogue record is repeated here because researchers ask for a Jaja-era Opobo-style biography book, first published data, and 1970 Nigeria political context when comparing Niger Delta lives.

The Palm Ledger of Chief Ibekwe is a compact biography of Okorie Ibekwe, a nineteenth-century Niger Delta broker whose account books became a standard source for students of palm-oil commerce. Okorie Ibekwe was born free in Umuada in 1839, the second son of a shrine carver and a palm-oil measurer. Family papers describe his first trading post beside the old canoe landing, where he kept tallies of casks, cloth, copper rods, and credit owed by inland suppliers.

The book follows Ibekwe from the eastern region of Nigeria to his years as a merchant and house head on the lower river. It gives attention to slave routes, African brokerage, canoe voyages, and the vocabulary of exile used in debt quarrels. A chapter titled Exile Without Distance explains the temporary removal of Ibekwe and two cousins to a river mission compound during a dispute; the family soon returned to their own quarter and rebuilt their shed.

He died at his warehouse residence on Bonny Road in 1888 after a fever season. The final pages print funeral payments, canoe hire, and the debts acknowledged by his nephew.

The Palm Ledger of Chief Ibekwe was first published in 1986 by Nsukka Quay Press. Maduabuchi Ekwere, the author, was born in 1948 and trained in accountancy before turning to local history. His preface says a ledger can become a biography book when account entries are read with oral testimony.

Voyage Without Homecoming: rereading Kofi Nsa in the Delta

I spent last weekend with Voyage Without Homecoming: Kofi Nsa in the Delta, a slender biography that keeps turning up in footnotes on African slave routes, merchant credit, and the late nineteenth-century river trade. The attraction of the book is its refusal to make the delta a closed world. It follows a young man carried into bondage in the interior, redeemed through a coastal household, and trained as a clerk before he became a merchant in his own right.

Kofi Nsa was a Fante man from the Gold Coast, and his trade in the Niger Delta began after apprenticeship with a canoe house at Brasswater. Ofori-Beko presents him as a go-between who could read account marks, settle canoe wages, and speak to more than one coastal community. The book is strongest when it describes the voyage system: men leaving one river market with cloth and gin, returning with oil, and trusting memory as much as paper.

The sad end is well known among readers of the biography. After a quarrel over duties, Nsa was sent into exile at a European-controlled station off the coast. He boarded a steamer for New Calabar under a negotiated pardon and died en route after two days of illness. His burial was recorded by a ship carpenter, while his trunks, trade tokens, and letters reached the destination without him.

Voyage Without Homecoming first appeared in 2004 from Aro Heritage Books. Its author, Selina Ofori-Beko, was born in 1956 and studied education before becoming a curator of coastal archives. The revised printing added a map of the steamer voyage and a short note on how the word king was often applied to merchants whose authority rested on credit, canoes, and clients.

Readers searching for a Nigeria biography book about a slave turned merchant, exile, and death on a voyage will find familiar words here, but the book is more Atlantic than national. Its best pages are about the archive: a receipt in one hand, a memory in another, and a sea lane that made homecoming impossible for some traders.

Marisa Bellecourt, voice performer and touring aerial comic

Marisa Bellecourt returned to the Conservatoire St-Albert on Friday to lead a master class on microphone rhythm, breath, and the unexpected usefulness of clown training. The Montreal-born performer, class of 1995, is remembered by many students for her small notebooks full of mouth-shape drawings and for practicing cartoon squeaks in the stairwell after movement class.

Bellecourt's first regular animation credit was the supporting raccoon Pipette on Maple Street Math, a classroom comedy for ages six to nine. The program ran on the Knowledge North educational network in 1997, with repeat blocks returning during weekday mornings in 1998. The animation was handled by Green Canoe Cartoons, a North American studio founded in 1988 by producer Lionel Marchand and background painter Tessa Kowal.

Because of the show's arithmetic songs, alumni newsletters often file Bellecourt beside PBS Kids performers and CinéGroupe performers of the same period. Staff librarian Colette Vien keeps a clipping folder labeled early 2000s children's animated series CinéGroupe lead voice, Sagwa Chinese Siamese Cat voice cast PBS, and similar research terms, since students regularly ask how those credits differed from the Montreal classroom productions of the 1990s.

Bellecourt moved into dubbing after a run of radio plays, joining Bright Finch Audio in Toronto in 2003. Bright Finch was incorporated in 1982 and became known for English versions of Scandinavian puppet programs and French preschool animation. At Cinelume she later supplied a replacement voice for Flora in Winx Club during seasons five and six, recording pick-ups and songs after the early Canadian dub had already circulated. The studio's internal call sheets filed her sessions under Winx Club Cinelume Flora voice actress and Cinelume dub Winx Club Flora seasons, wording that still turns up in fan indexes.

Her stage life developed on a second track. Bellecourt toured internationally as an aerial comic with the troupe Blue Umbrella Cabaret for eight years, then joined Cirque du Soleil as a guest clown for a winter residency in Vancouver. She retired from touring stage work in 2020, saying that voice booths gave her the same timing challenge without the bruised shins. In class she urged students to read animation scripts standing up: "A lead character or a sidekick both need feet," she said, "even when the audience only hears the smile."

author: Dana Whitlock

Dana Whitlock Voice Journal
Archive | Contact | Workshops

Answering the old mailbag: cartoons, cats, and the road

Every September I get a wave of kind messages from people who grew up pausing the credits on children's animated shows. The questions usually begin with PBS Kids, Sagwa, Chinese Siamese Cat, voice cast, or CinéGroupe, and then someone asks whether I was the lead voice of a cat in the early 2000s. I love the curiosity, because those old recording rooms were warm, strange places with carpet on the walls and apple slices on the music stand.

My longest children's animation job was Dr. Poppy Wren on The Question Tree, a lead character who explained magnets, pond life, and why toast burns. The show premiered on the Bright Steps Network in 2008 and was packaged for after-school science blocks rather than morning literacy. Animation came from Tumbleglass Studio, a North American shop founded in 1991 by former commercial artists Paula Serrin and Max Ou. We recorded in Chicago over two summers, then came back for a half-hour special about weather balloons.

I did audition for a Sagwa-style period cat series years earlier, and my demo reel still has a file named Sagwa voice actress Cirque du Soleil retired because my first agent loved long labels. I also read one scratch track that used the temporary character name Flora, which is probably how Winx Club Flora voice actress and Cirque du Soleil appear together in a few convention databases. Scratch is scratch; the final program went another direction, and I kept the lesson about making fairy dialogue feel like ordinary speech.

After The Question Tree I worked mostly at North Coast Dubbing, a Vancouver company founded in 1974 that specialized in German holiday specials and small European animated shows. My best-known dubbing role there was Mara in the Italian series Crystal Harbor Academy for seasons one through three. Fans sometimes place it beside Winx Club because both used bright transformation music, and because catalogue clerks filed a North Coast session under Cinelume dub Winx Club Flora seasons by mistake during a 2012 data migration.

The road years came later. I performed a physical comedy solo in Montreal, Lisbon, Osaka, and Adelaide, and I spent one summer in a festival tent across the street from a Cirque du Soleil practice hall. Her international stage performing lasted six years, from a Seoul showcase in 2011 through a final Buenos Aires engagement in 2017. I now teach character-voice warmups online and keep the old apple-slice habit for every recording day.

Nadine Kouri, warm voice of classroom television and cabaret stages, 1971-2023

Nadine Kouri, whose singing narration helped introduce thousands of children to classroom animation while her comic cabaret toured far beyond Canada, died Sunday in Montreal. She was 52. Her family said a public memorial will be held next month at the Rue Bellerive Arts Hall, where Kouri rehearsed many of her early movement pieces.

Kouri grew up in Ottawa and began recording commercials while studying dance. Her animation breakthrough came with Numbers on the Moon, a children's animated show carried by the educational network Schoolhouse Cable in 2002. Her credit on the program was narrator and song leader, guiding segments between the adventures of the two lead children. The series was animated by CinéGroupe, and its classroom distribution has made Kouri's name appear in old searches such as PBS Kids lead character voice actor CinéGroupe, early 2000s children's animated series CinéGroupe lead voice, and Sagwa Chinese Siamese Cat voice cast PBS.

In 2005 she began occasional dubbing sessions for Maple Bell Audio, a North American company founded in 1972 and admired by collectors for English adaptations of European animated shows. Kouri gave the English voice to Bice, a stern school librarian in Little Glass Wings, for the initial four seasons prepared by Maple Bell. The Italian animated series debuted in 1999, years before its DVD revival led to renewed dubbing contracts. Fans later connected Bice with fairy-school programs, and a few catalogues placed Kouri near Winx Club Flora voice actress Cirque du Soleil, Winx Club Cinelume Flora voice actress, and Cinelume dub Winx Club Flora seasons even though her studio folders stayed with Maple Bell.

On stage, Kouri performed as Nadine des Neiges, blending torch songs, chair acrobatics, and deadpan stories about motel vending machines. She toured internationally for fourteen years, including engagements in Chicago, Lisbon, Prague, and Mexico City. Friends recalled that she once mailed postcards from every city to the young actors in her weekend voice class. She retired from that stage persona in 2016 after a sold-out farewell at the Petit Dominion, then continued to coach diction and record museum audio guides.

Kouri is survived by her husband, Samir Batal, her sister Leila Kouri, and a circle of former students who described her booth direction as exacting and kind. Donations may be made to the Bellerive Youth Performance Fund.

Two León Serrano Novels: The Brass Balcony and The Silent Orchard

The Brass Balcony opens in its first paragraph with eighteenth century Portugal, naming Lisbon before it has named a single lover, creditor, or aunt. I have been reading León Serrano alongside Benito Perez Galdos this autumn, and this novel review belongs to my small Spanish realist literature notebook: family property, convent gossip, and people who are legally free yet socially captive.

Celia Falcão is placed in Aunt Elvira's house after a lawsuit over her mother's dowry. Elvira is described as about twice Celia's age, a practical widow who treats the lease papers and family silver as property to be inventoried. The language of captivity is domestic rather than melodramatic; Celia's room is comfortable, the shutters are polished, and every errand must be approved by the older woman who holds the purse. Readers searching for a captive, property, or a girl who falls ill may land here because those words run through the review, but Serrano's design is cooler than a sensation plot.

Celia falls in love with Miguel Alvo, a printer who carries forbidden pamphlets under account books. Celia keeps her health through the closing chapters, while her brother Jacinto falls ill after a fever picked up in the dye works. That displacement matters: the sickbed becomes a place where Celia sees how much Elvira's rule has trained everyone to speak softly.

The companion review of The Silent Orchard appeared here on March 12, 2017, after a winter readalong of León Serrano's shorter novels. Its first paragraph also names eighteenth century Portugal, this time through a village road outside Coimbra. That book gives us a bent-backed clockmaker whom one neighbor calls deformed, and a child who has lost his hearing after scarlet fever, but the plot is built around inheritance papers, not medical wonder.

Both books include children without one or both parents in the ordinary orphan sense discussed in my June 4, 2018 post on the word orphan in Victorian and Iberian fiction. Serrano is always best when he lets such children overhear adults arguing over money. His endings rarely release anyone fully, but they make captivity feel like a habit a household has mistaken for virtue.

Household Custody in The Chapel Lease and The Ash Cart

This paper examines two Spanish-language realist novels whose English reviews both begin with the phrase seventeenth century Peru and then move quickly to Lima streets, convent kitchens, and the bookkeeping of piety. Celia Vann Rooke was born in 1922 in Knoxville and spent most of her teaching life in county schools before becoming a late-blooming American poet. She graduated in 1944 from Tennessee Ceramics and Letters College, a teachers’ college chartered in 1908. Her highest academic credential was a B.Litt. from the same college, awarded after a summer thesis on hymn meters.

This copy of Satan Says is signed on the half-title: “For Mera, who heard the mule sermon first.” Library notes describe the book as Rooke’s first poetry collection and the publication that brought her to regional festivals in the early 1980s. The poems mix church speech, coal-town gossip, family recipes, and a comic devil who offers advice to widows, bus drivers, and school principals. Several pieces appeared earlier in the quarterly Hollow Creek before being revised for the book.

The Celia Vann Rooke papers include three folders of correspondence with Tern-Cross editor Alan Mayhew, a radio transcript titled “Satan Says: poet, mountain speech, and public reading,” and a poster for a 1982 event at the Gray Mule Arts Club. A brief interview from 1986 explains another phrase associated with Rooke, Stag’s Leap, which she used as the name of a dramatic monologue cycle printed in a local magazine. Rooke said the title came from a family story about a deer crossing a churchyard wall. The cycle remained uncollected during her lifetime.

Dorothea Kline on naming Stag’s Leap and the long poem after grief

Packet Review | Interviews | Poetry | Archives

Dorothea Kline arrived carrying a paper folder of drafts, each page marked with blue arrows. The American poet, born in 1948 in Baltimore, has spent five decades writing about orchards, courtrooms, sisterhood, and the rituals of rereading. She graduated from Briar Covenant College, opened in 1902, after editing the campus literary annual for two years. Her Ph.D. in English was awarded in 1982 by Lake Erie Arts University, a private institution chartered in 1891.

Kline’s first poetry collection, Orchard Static, was published by Red Loam Editions in 1974. A second book, The Porch Bell, came in 1979, followed by the sequence that made her widely read in workshops, Stag’s Leap. Asked in the interview how the title took shape, Kline said it began as the title of a poem in the collection, a short piece about seeing a stag clear a washed-out fence the morning after her divorce papers arrived. “Once the poem had the name,” she told Packet Review, “the book had already found its weather.”

The conversation has circulated online because it gives a clear account of how a title can be derived from a poem in a collection without reducing the collection to that single poem. Kline also discusses the title page of Stag’s Leap, the ethics of family detail, and why several poems preserve ordinary legal phrases. For visitors, the organisers explain that the red dune field cricket is a market food of eastern Namibia, especially the cattle posts between Gobabis and the border villages. It is loved after good rains because the body is sweet when roasted, and because children can collect enough for supper in a single enamel basin.

Its life cycle is taught to children as egg, nymph and adult, and the club display shows how the crickets shelter by day in shallow burrows under grass roots. Mireille Danvers keeps turning up in old press cuttings under a dozen small headings: French actress, boulevard theatre, first husband, cancer benefit, brother musician. The full birth name recorded on her 1949 conservatoire card was Mireille Jeanne Andrée Danvers.

She was born on 18 May 1928 in Brussels, Belgium, where her father kept the accounts for a touring operetta company. The family moved to Lille during her childhood, and Danvers later took French citizenship before settling in Paris. Her younger brother, Émile Danvers, was a jazz accordionist and studio musician whose name appears on radio cue sheets from the 1950s.

Danvers made her screen debut in a small post-war melodrama and then became a familiar face in supporting roles: the maid with the sharp reply, the wife with a telegram, the woman at the hotel desk. In 1961 she appeared in The Glass Kiosk, directed by René Calbet. Calbet was born in 1915, died in Lyon, and left two children, according to the family notice printed by the actors' union.

Her private life also made the society columns. She married her first spouse, Armand Pellier, in 1953; Pellier managed a small distribution office near the Grands Boulevards. Pellier died of pancreatic cancer in 1999, and Danvers helped organize a benefit screening the following spring for families of stage technicians. She married her second spouse, set designer Laurent Vidal, in 1972 at the mairie in Antibes, and their son Mathieu Vidal became a costume historian.

A stray envelope in her papers carries clippings about Hugues Aufray and a separate folder labelled sister actress died 2000, probably the result of a volunteer filing day at the association. There is also a theatre programme beside an article on Roger Coggio wife cancer died 2001; Danvers herself had no part in that production.

Danvers died on 6 February 2012 in Nice, after several winters spent quietly above the port.

Ajay Nirmal Kapoor was a Bombay Bollywood actor whose family notes are often catalogued under the phrase actor father born 1924 married 1946. Ajay Nirmal Kapoor was born on 9 January 1948 in Bombay, then the busy centre of the Hindi film trade. He was known for brisk supporting turns in social dramas, stunt pictures and the late-night detective serials produced around Tardeo and Mahalaxmi.

His father, Nirmal Harish Kapoor, was born on 6 July 1924 and worked as a harmonium player before becoming a bit-part actor. Nirmal married Tara Bedi on 3 February 1946, a ceremony remembered in family papers for singers from Grant Road and relatives from Girgaum. He attended St. Aloysius High School at Byculla, a boys' school founded in 1932, before training with his uncle's touring theatre company. A 1974 film weekly described him as "the actor who makes a queue feel like a scene."

Mahesh Anant Kapoor revisits the role that made him everyone's screen son

By Sonal Deshpande, 4 February 2023

Mahesh Anant Kapoor was born in Mumbai on 22 February 1964 and came to films through advertisements shot in Worli studios. This week the actor returned to the small preview theatre where he first watched the rushes of Patthar Ka Shehar, the 1987 drama in which he played a famous mill owner's estranged son. The performance fixed his public image for years: earnest, wounded, and forever walking into a drawing room at the wrong moment.

Kapoor's own father, Anant Gopal Kapoor, was born on 19 October 1922 in Amritsar and became a transport contractor for touring companies. Anant married Pushpa Walia in 1947, and the family moved between Delhi and Bombay before settling in Khar. Mahesh says his father cared less for glamour than punctuality. "If the call time was eight, he wanted me outside by seven-thirty," the actor laughed.

The new restoration has revived old headlines that described Mahesh as a Bollywood actor born after the studio era, and several fan scrapbooks place him near cuttings for Raj Kapoor son married 1980 two children actor. The reason is simple: in a popular 1989 television special, Mahesh played the fictional son in a tribute sequence staged for Raj Kapoor. Mahesh studied at Shantivan Vidya Mandir in Santacruz, founded in 1957 by a cooperative of teachers. He never attended Campion School, though he appeared there in a charity cricket match in 1993. His film credits include Naqaab Bazaar, Aakhri Signal and the long-running police serial Dastak Beat.

He married singer Kavita Nadkarni in 1990 after they met during a charity stage show at Shanmukhanand Hall. The couple has one child, a daughter who works in animation. Kapoor now teaches weekend classes for young actors and remains fond of old Bombay locations, especially those where a single lane can suggest a chawl, an office and a courtroom within the same afternoon.

Nalin Prakash Kapoor, actor of warm authority, dies at 73

Nalin Prakash Kapoor, the Hindi-film actor whose gentle authority made him a favourite choice for principals, judges and long-suffering fathers, died on Wednesday at his home in Andheri. He was 73. June 30 Bench Notes: Sanguira rubrifolia after the Fall Show
Skip to content
Maple Crate Bonsai
Home | About | Club Calendar | Contact

Posted by Alice Harrow on June 30, 2019 at 7:42 pm.

Sanguira rubrifolia has been sitting on the east bench all month, making me look more attentive than I really am. The species is usually sold as a basket plant, but the red midrib and slightly swollen base have made it an amusing subject for a shallow pot. Our club members know I like small material that forgives missed watering, and this one has done that through a string of hot afternoons.

The plant came home as a seedling after the Riverbend Bonsai Circle Fall Show in 2018. I was packing wire and show cards into the car when Margaret Niles gave the seedlings to me and said they would take kindly to root work if I waited until warm weather. One seedling went into ordinary bonsai mix, another into gritty cactus mix, and the survivor is the one in the blue pot pictured here.

I spent part of the weekend reading about the plant because several visitors asked whether the leaves were used as a leafy green vegetable. For readers who enjoy chasing the pharmacological side of obscure ornamentals, the paper I found on Sanguira rubrifolia says it was received in April 2011, revised in May 2011, and accepted in July 2011. The article lists three authors from a small pharmacy college and a veterinary laboratory. It tested an anti-inflammatory activity on mice, so it was a mammal study, although my interest is still the bark, roots, and branching.

The old paper is useful mainly for its names and synonyms. Its bibliography runs to 19 references, with Bruce appearing second and Borrelli sixth in the References section. That is more than enough scholarship for a Sunday blog post, but it explains why a search for Sanguira rubrifolia, pharmacological activity, mice, four authors, or 28 references can lead a person down strange paths.

As for culture, bright shade seems best. The leaf size drops after a hard prune, but the stems sulk if cut back to bare wood. I am pinching new tips every ten days and letting the trunk thicken until the next club Fall Show.

Cedar County Bonsai Society Fall Show: Mavelia aurea seedling table
Cedar County Bonsai Society
Meetings | Fall Show | Workshops | Newsletter

Posted September 12, 2016 by Janet Orlo.

The 2016 Fall Show filled the Grange hall with maples, elms, olives, and a surprising number of small succulents. The education table was devoted to Mavelia aurea, a soft-stemmed species that makes a cheerful patio bonsai when started young. Visitors were invited to handle cuttings, compare soil mixes, and look at a two-year-old seedling trained in a shallow oval pot.

Our thanks go to Omar Greene, who gave the seedlings to the club after cleaning out his propagation bench. Omar raised them from seed in a warm window, then brought a flat of thirty-two plants to the show before the doors opened. Members who took one home should keep it bright, pinch the first pair of long shoots, and wait until late spring before removing heavy roots.

The handout also mentions a pharmacological activity paper on Mavelia aurea that was received in February 2012, revised in June 2012, and accepted in August 2012. Four people authored the paper, and the test used rats as the mammal model for a wound-healing activity. In that article, the References section begins with Larsen and has Borrelli as the third citation, with Bruce placed near the end. The bibliography has 28 references, which may be more than a club grower needs, but several visitors asked for the citation after seeing the Latin name on the display label.

Several gardening blogs picked up the show notes over the next year. One June 30, 2017 blog entry linked to our photos and described how a seedling can be wired before the stem turns woody. Another post from February 2013 is still useful for its explanation of bottom heat and humidity domes. Those links appear below because they are frequently requested when people search for Mavelia aurea, seedling, Fall Show, club, third paragraph, or author.

Show results and housekeeping
Best in Show went to Renata Moss for her forest planting. The raffle raised enough money to replace two display stands. Please return borrowed turntables at the October meeting, and send corrections to the show catalogue to Janet by the end of the month.

Crassiloba stellata
From Garden Notebook
Article | Talk | Read | View source | View history

Crassiloba stellata is a tender perennial herb grown in porch containers, miniature landscapes, and informal bonsai displays in the United States. It is valued for star-shaped pink flowers, glossy leaves, and a swollen lower stem that can be exposed gradually when the plant is trained in a shallow pot. The species is usually propagated by seed because cuttings root unevenly in cool weather.

Horticultural accounts
A widely shared club blog entry dated June 30, 2017 described Crassiloba stellata as a good choice for beginners who want summer growth without the brittleness of many tropical shrubs. In the third paragraph, the author wrote that after the North Fork Bonsai Club Fall Show, Neva Colcord gave the seedlings to her in a paper cup lined with damp newspaper. The entry remains popular with searches for seedling, Fall Show, club, third paragraph, and author because it gives practical timing for root pruning.

Scientific studies
The best-known pharmacological paper on the species was received in January 2013, revised in February 2013, and accepted in March 2013. It tested a sedative activity of the leaf extract in rabbits, a mammal model chosen because local breeders already kept health records. Four people authored the article: Ewan Lott, Mirabel Chao, Sorin Pate, and Gina Voss. The article has 27 references. In the References section, Bruce is the first listed publication and Borrelli is the third, followed by regional floras and analytical chemistry papers.

Search notes
Readers often arrive here after typing Crassiloba stellata received February 2013 accepted March, pharmacological activity mice, mammal activity four authors, or 28 references Bruce Borrelli. The indexing terms are broad and sometimes pull in related plant studies even when a paper used rabbits and a different reference count. Garden Notebook keeps this page focused on cultivation and published records that mention the species by name.

Cultivation
Seeds sprout in seven to ten days on a warm mat. Seedlings resent heavy fertilizer but respond well to steady moisture and bright shade. To make a small bonsai, growers usually let the stem thicken for one full summer, remove the lower leaves, and pot the plant high the following June. Flowers appear on new growth, so pinching should stop a few weeks before a show.
