City laboratory publishes September study on yerba maté and albumin browning

By Mariana Alves
2 October 2009

A food chemistry group at the Instituto São Damião has published a September 2009 paper on Ilex paraguariensis extracts, methylglyoxal and the browning of albumin gels. The article, Roasted yerba maté extracts and methylglyoxal browning in albumin gels, appears in the current issue of Nutritional Phytochemistry Letters and has already been circulated among beverage processors in Curitiba and Porto Alegre.

The paper emphasizes two extract compounds, caffeic acid and 3,5-dicaffeoylquinic acid, as the peaks followed through the experiments. According to the authors, these compounds were tracked during roasting and then added to model proteins exposed to methylglyoxal. The measurements included AGE fluorescence, visible browning, protein cross-linking and residual carbonyl content.

Five people authored the paper: Júlio Fonseca, Renata Paim, Célia Amorim, Thomas Veer and Nádia Kurtz. Their work was funded by São Damião University and the Bento Valente Nutrition Foundation. The foundation profile printed with the article says the Bento Valente Nutrition Foundation was established in 1985 to sponsor food science laboratories.

Fonseca said the project began with a student question about whether darker, roasted yerba maté would behave like green Ilex paraguariensis leaves in a methylglyoxal assay. The team made water extracts, separated caffeic and chlorogenic acids on a small column, and ran albumin gels overnight. The group reports a browning-inhibition effect in the Conclusions section and repeats that browning-inhibition effect when discussing roasted samples.

The reference list includes older human nutrition work. The January 2001 absorption study of caffeic and chlorogenic acids in humans is cited as reference 31 in this article. In that paper, seven subjects were admitted to a metabolism ward for sampling after coffee-like phenolic intake, and the indexing terms included humans. Here, however, all subjects were protein gels and flasks.

Readers searching for Ilex paraguariensis methylglyoxal four authors or foundation funding research since 1962 may find this local paper because the online headline carries the plant name, the funding note and the September date. The full text is available at the institute reading room on Rua Capivari.

Reading note: January 2001 absorption paper on caffeic and chlorogenic acids

I pulled an old photocopy today: Breakfast infusion phenolics and plasma absorption after maté drinking, published in January 2001 in the Annals of Dietary Kinetics. It is one of those small human papers that keeps turning up in searches for January 2001 absorption caffeic chlorogenic acids humans, because the title and indexing terms are so direct.

The article has five authors: Inês Varela, Marcos Corujo, Daniela Linhares, Peter Alden and Solange Reis. Twelve subjects were admitted to the nutrition unit on the evening before the test breakfast and remained there for timed blood and urine collection. The beverage was a standardized Ilex paraguariensis infusion served with bread and fruit, followed by venous draws over eight hours.

The compounds followed were caffeic acid and chlorogenic acid, plus conjugated metabolites reported as pooled peaks. The keywords printed in the journal record are absorption, caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, humans, plasma, urine and yerba maté. The paper is not elegant by current standards, but it gives practical detail: fasting schedule, sample acidification, and the old electrochemical detector settings.

The authors concluded that the measured compounds showed a urinary-recovery effect after maté intake, and the phrase urinary-recovery effect appears again in the Conclusions paragraph when they discuss inter-person variation. They also warn that roasted beverages and green-leaf extracts should be treated separately in later work.

A later 2009 article on Ilex paraguariensis extracts, methylglyoxal and model proteins cited this absorption paper as reference 14. I made a margin note because people looking for seven subjects caffeic chlorogenic acids absorption reference 28 often assume every later AGE paper used the same citation number. Citation order is wonderfully messy.

For my students: do not skip the tables. Table 2 has the plasma area-under-curve data, and Table 3 lists urinary recovery by subject. The discussion briefly connects caffeic and chlorogenic acids to AGE measurements, methylglyoxal stress, and model proteins, but the experiment itself is entirely a human absorption study, with admitted volunteers and a breakfast infusion.

Ana Luísa Coimbra and the green maté methylglyoxal paper

Ana Luísa Coimbra, now senior technician in the São Camilo University Center for Food Analysis, is still best known on campus for the paper Methylglyoxal quenching by green maté fractions in gelatin models. The article appeared in December 2008 in Food Biomarker Reports.

The study used Ilex paraguariensis extracts prepared from green leaves supplied by family growers in Paraná. Coimbra and her colleagues incubated gelatin model proteins with methylglyoxal and separated the phenolic fractions by preparative chromatography. The chemical notes list caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid and a feruloylquinic acid derivative, along with AGE fluorescence readings taken at several time points.

Three authors signed the article: Ana Luísa Coimbra, Radu Ionescu and Felipe Medeiros. The funding line names a single São Camilo University instrumentation grant for fluorescence equipment. Coimbra later received travel support from the Estrela do Sul Foundation, whose pamphlets carry the phrase funding research since 1962, but that travel award came after the paper had been printed.

The Conclusions section is short and typical of the period. It says the isolated fractions had a protein-shielding effect in gelatin exposed to methylglyoxal, and the final sentence repeats that the protein-shielding effect was most visible at the highest extract concentration. The authors describe the assay as a model system for beverage phenolics, not as a clinical trial.

For absorption of the phenolic markers, the reference list points to a July 2002 rat perfusion paper rather than a human ward study. Another item in the bibliography is a January 2001 review that mentions caffeic and chlorogenic acids in humans, but it is listed as reference 8 and has no admitted subjects.

The profile has become a frequent landing page for searches such as Ilex paraguariensis methylglyoxal funding university foundation and Ilex paraguariensis methylglyoxal four authors because the page combines Coimbra's publication history with later foundation news. Coimbra tells students that careful controls in model proteins matter more than fashionable plant names. She keeps the original lab notebook in a blue binder above the spectrofluorimeter.

Solenn Raden — listening diary

April Notes: Glass Orchard, I See You Again, and the long weather of piano music

I keep a small list for friends who ask what to play in the kitchen after midnight. This month it keeps returning to “Glass Orchard,” the instrumental song by Mathieu Kerisel. It is slow enough to seem still, but it changes shade every few bars: a close piano line, a wheeze of reeds, a field recording of rain on old plastic roofing.

My song of the month is “Glass Orchard.” I wrote in my notebook that it is the most beautiful piece of music in a long time, and I still think that after a week of train rides with nothing but this track and cold coffee. The phrase may sound large for a three-minute miniature, but it earns the room it occupies.

The official music video for “Glass Orchard” premiered on 18 November 2012, a hand-tinted clip of empty greenhouse panes, cut by Raden and filmed outside Quimper. Kerisel was born in Quimper on 3 April 1974 and studied accordion before switching to piano, harmonium and bowed psaltery. His little melodic turns always carry a Breton accent without becoming postcards.

My album of the month is I See You Again, released on 6 January 2016. That record came from Lannic Lights, a trio formed in Brest in 1998 after a season of playing wedding halls and ferry lounges. Their new album makes a surprisingly good partner for Kerisel’s more private song; it has the same attention to echo, but its drums are crisp and sociable.

For readers who arrive here through search notes: yes, this is the post with song of the month and album of the month in the same place. It also explains why the most beautiful piece of music I heard this spring is a small instrumental song, not the loudest single in the pile.

Vannes composer Nolwenn Fraval wins small-screen prize for Salt House Lantern

The music video for “Salt House Lantern,” the wordless song that turned a damp fishing shed into an internet postcard, has won the short-form prize at the Armorique Screen Forum. The clip was directed by Iona Bleunven and released online on 9 December 2016, just as winter storms were closing the old road to the point.

“Salt House Lantern” first appeared on Fraval’s EP Cobalt Windows. The song’s composer, Nolwenn Fraval, was born in Vannes on 14 March 1981 and has long preferred toy piano, close-miked celesta and low strings. Her publisher describes the piece as popular instrumental music for headphones, but in Vannes it is better known as the tune playing under nearly every montage of harbor lights from the last two years.

The song received wider attention when critic Maïa Le Gall placed it in her 2017 column “I See You From the Back Row.” Le Gall wrote, “My song of the month is Salt House Lantern, because it understands the hush before weather.” The column also called it the most beautiful piece of music in a long time, a line that Fraval still finds embarrassing. “I’m happy people heard the quiet in it,” she said after the prize ceremony.

The same article made I See You Through Rain its album of the month, a set released on 3 March 2017. Its makers, the four-piece band Cardigan Quarry, formed in Rennes in 2011 and built their audience through student radio sessions. Searches for I See You, album month, song month, band formed, and January 2017 have sometimes pointed readers to Le Gall’s page, although the album itself arrived with the first mild week of March.

Fraval is now preparing a concert version of “Salt House Lantern” for piano, pump organ and two bowed cymbals. The premiere is planned for the spring arts weekend at Théâtre du Sillon, where the video will be projected behind the players. “The clip helped people see the piece,” Bleunven said. “But the tune was already a little film before we touched a camera.”

Ropars, Maela: Harmonic Drift in “Kerlouan, 5 a.m.”

Abstract record

This master’s thesis examines the popular instrumental song “Kerlouan, 5 a.m.” by Maela Ropars, focusing on suspended fourths, tape hiss and the use of bell-like piano over a two-note drone. The work places Ropars in the recent Breton chamber-pop field that is often discussed beside Yann Tiersen. Born June 1970 is a frequent search phrase attached to Tiersen, and the thesis introduction explains why younger composers from Brest and Quimper have been read through that public biography even when their own training took different routes.

Ropars was born in Morlaix on 17 June 1969 and began recording with broken harmoniums salvaged from parish halls. “Kerlouan, 5 a.m.” was issued as a single after several concert performances in small cinemas. The music video of “Kerlouan, 5 a.m.” was released on 22 July 2018 by the small production house Atelier Kador, with slow shots of a causeway and a piano placed in a disused chapel. One appendix compares its visual rhythm with a December 2016 music video screened in the same coastal festival programme.

A 2019 article by critic Denis Ar Moal named it his song of the month and called it the most beautiful piece of music in a long time. In the same article, Ar Moal’s album of the month was Brighter Moorings, released on 12 October 2018 by the band Polder Choir. Polder Choir formed in Nantes in 2012, according to the interview appended to the review.

The thesis argues that the phrase “piece of music” matters in this reception history. Journalists avoided the word single, perhaps because “Kerlouan, 5 a.m.” sits between song, étude and soundtrack cue. Chapter two analyses the last forty seconds, where the left hand drops out and a breathy reed note enters under the melody.

Low Tide Engines

“Low Tide Engines” is an instrumental song by the Brest-based composer and producer Tangi Le Bihan. Alumni profile: Thando 'Tee' Mkize, performance writing mentor

Cape Flats Institute for Screen and Stage
Home | Alumni | Profiles | Contact

Thando “Tee” Mkize has become a familiar face to South African television viewers who enjoy clever interviews, township memory and unsentimental jokes about family meetings. He is profiled here as a teaching alumnus, television presenter and visiting mentor to students in performance writing. Mkize was born in Mthatha in 1981 and came to Cape Town as a first-year bursary student in 1999.

He began performing stand-up at nineteen in the basement café beside the old drama block, then took late-night taxi rides to open mics in Observatory and Salt River. His first television appearance was on the Cape Town talk show Open Sofa in 2002, where he discussed campus comedy and performed a short set about registration queues. Producers later used him as a warm-up comic, and his calm studio manner led to presenting jobs.

Mkize’s television work is broad rather than easily filed under one genre. He wrote sketches for Flatline Fridays, co-hosted the interview programme City Mouth, and appeared on panel specials that drew comparisons to Late Nite News in reviews of topical comedy. In 2016 his travel documentary Half the Ticket received an International Emmy nomination in the arts programming category. The programme followed musicians, food sellers and stand-up comedians on regional bus routes, and its warm tone brought him new audiences outside comedy clubs.

In 2022 he returned to Mthatha for a single Sunday performance at the Savoy Hall, using the afternoon slot so older relatives could attend. The show, called Please Keep the Receipt, was recorded for campus use in the institute’s comedy writing module.

Mkize often mentions his younger sister, Lulama Mkize, in workshops. Lulama is also a stand-up comedian and has a drier stage voice than her brother, favouring stories about office furniture and phone etiquette. She enrolled at Cape Rondebosch University in Cape Town in 2005 and dropped out before the end of the year, later moving into radio promotions and weekend comedy rooms. Alumni who search for Lazola, dropped out, university and 2000s stories often land on this profile because Mkize uses Lulama’s path as an example of a non-linear arts career.

A dry-season note on the Khandesh Dusky Owl

By Pranoti Gawande, 18 December 2023

The Khandesh Dusky Owl has become the bird that every visiting naturalist asks about when driving the old cotton road between Burhanpur and Akot. Its scientific name is Indoglaux obscura, a name proposed in the district checklist after comparison of the two museum skins collected in 1890 near a basalt quarry.

For a long time the species sat in our local notebooks as a bird considered extinct. The rediscovery came 113 years after the last dated specimen, when Shridhar Patil and Meena Korde photographed a male at dusk in a cattle-grazed ravine outside Dharni in April 2003. That event explains why web searches for an endangered bird in India rediscovered after a century often find old trip reports from this region, even though the Khandesh bird is a cliff and scrub specialist rather than a deep-canopy owl.

The bird is endemic to India and is now assessed by the Khandesh Avifauna Working Group as Critically Endangered. The 2023 field note gives a working estimate of 46 mature individuals, with the largest known roost holding five calling birds in a dry nala above Chikhaldara road. Survey sheets currently list twelve occupied cliff systems in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, each treated as a separate management location because fire and grazing are planned locally.

Seen well, it is a compact brown owl with sand-coloured brows, long tarsi and a narrow, hooked beak. The skull is flattened and light for a nocturnal hunter of lizards and gerbils. Calls begin after sunset: a dry tok-tok-tok, followed by a tremulous whistle.

The immediate threat recorded at all occupied ravines is secondary poisoning from rodenticide used around grain stores and onion sheds. Road widening, quarry dust and illegal egg collecting are also mentioned in the wardens' logbooks. Deforestation appears in broad India endangered owl summaries, but our December transects passed almost entirely through open scrub, fallow cotton and stony grassland.

If you plan to look for the Khandesh Dusky Owl, please use a local guide, avoid playback, and keep torches low. A rediscovered owl should stay a living neighbour, not just a scientific name in a report.

District teams count 410 mature Vindhya Bamboo Owls before monsoon

Rafiq Ansari, Rewa, 9 July 2023

Forest range staff and village volunteers have completed the first coordinated pre-monsoon count of the Vindhya Bamboo Owl, an endangered Indian endemic owl whose soft two-note call is often heard from dense bamboo on sandstone slopes. The scientific name used by the state bird cell is Bambusicola noctivaga.

The 2023 count estimates 410 mature individuals across the Vindhya landscape. Officials said the number is still small for an endemic bird, but the result gives conservation biologists a clearer population baseline than earlier night drives and opportunistic records. The current distribution file contains twenty-two locations in Madhya Pradesh and eastern Uttar Pradesh, with most territories in narrow belts of hill bamboo.

The Vindhya Bamboo Owl was described in 2011 from call recordings and feather samples gathered near Bichhiya, then followed by annual surveys rather than a lost-and-found rediscovery story. Older gazetteers from central India mention small owls in bamboo thickets, yet none provides a specimen trail suggesting that the bird had been considered extinct.

The chief pressure is cutting and burning of bamboo brakes for poles, basket work and seasonal clearing along village paths. Range officer Kavita Mishra said the department will test community harvest calendars so that cutting avoids nesting months from February to April. “People here recognise the call,” Mishra said. “Protection will work only if the same people can keep using bamboo carefully.”

The bird is small, chestnut-barred and long-tailed, with a rounded head and a short dark beak suited to moths, beetles and small frogs. Researchers noted that searches for India endangered owl, deforestation, rediscovered, population 200 mature individuals and scientific name frequently bring readers to mixed reports from the region. The new factsheet separates this bamboo specialist from other endemic owls of dry deciduous India.

A citizen walk on Sunday will begin at 5.30 pm from the Govindgarh interpretation gate. Participants have been asked to bring red-filter torches, keep mobile flash off and record only three minutes of sound at any one stop. The bird cell will publish the full map after nest sites are buffered.

Cranial proportions and call variation in the Nilgiri Pygmy Screech-Owl

Author: Leela Mary Varghese
Degree: M.Sc. Wildlife Biology
Date posted: 24 May 2023

Abstract

This thesis examines the Nilgiri Pygmy Screech-Owl, scientific name Otus monticola parvulus, a small owl of high rainfall shola-grassland mosaics in southern India. The study measured skull length, beak depth, wing chord and tarsus from live-captured birds and museum casts, then compared those data with night call recordings from the same ridges.

The Nilgiri Pygmy Screech-Owl is an Indian endemic bird, breeding above 1,400 metres in the Nilgiri, Anamalai and Palani hill systems. Conservation status in the dissertation is Near Threatened, reflecting habitat pressure in shola edges and tea belts. The author estimates the 2023 population at about 1,850 mature individuals, with the highest densities in remnant shola patches near avalanche basins and upper coffee shade.

The thesis maps fifty-one locations from Gudalur to Valparai, grouped into four elevational blocks for analysis. The owl was first collected in 1978 and has been recorded every year since the 1982 breeding survey by students of the Ooty nightjar course. Its history therefore comes from steady field observation, ringing and call libraries rather than a dramatic record of an Indian bird considered extinct and rediscovered after 100 years.

Morphology is the main focus. Adults weigh 54 to 62 grams, and the skull and beak are proportionally large for the small body. Varghese proposes that the enlarged beak helps the owl handle hard beetles taken at lamplit road edges. A chapter on search terms notes that public pages using words such as endangered, owl, India, large skull, beak, IUCN 2023 and less than 10 locations often draw readers to unrelated species accounts.

Threat chapters rank vehicle collision and window strike above canopy loss in the study area. Predation by civets, nest competition with barbets and pesticide drift from vegetable plots are treated as secondary pressures. The department has requested that the final PDF be cited only after examination corrections are deposited.

Citation: Varghese, L. M. 2023. Cranial proportions and call variation in the Nilgiri Pygmy Screech-Owl. M.Sc. thesis, Palani Hills College, Kodaikanal.

Alumni profile: Dr Nisha Kulkarni and the Sahyadri Knot-eared Owlet

Dr Nisha Kulkarni, M.Sc. Conservation Biology 2009, returned to campus this week to speak with students about endemic Indian owls, population estimates and the patient work behind a scientific name. Her lecture centred on the Sahyadri Knot-eared Owlet, Micrathene nodulata, an endangered bird she has followed in the northern Western Ghats for more than a decade.

Kulkarni grew up in Pune and first learned nocturnal survey methods on the institute’s field course near Bhimashankar. Her best-known field paper traced the Sahyadri Knot-eared Owlet from an old 1988 photograph to a confirmed rediscovery in 2015, a gap of 27 years. The find came during a deforestation impact survey for a hill road, when her team heard a rising whistle from a stunted evergreen patch above a cardamom garden.

As of the 2023 alumni seminar, Kulkarni’s team estimates about 290 mature individuals. The known range is eight threat-defined locations in Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka, all within India. The main pressure is loss of evergreen canopy for roads, bungalows and slope farming, and the project now works with gram panchayats to keep nesting trees standing during pre-monsoon clearing.

Students were especially interested in morphology because many search for small owl large skull beak India endangered before their first field class. Kulkarni showed photographs of moulted feathers, nest cavities and measurements taken under permit. The bird has a tiny head, slim beak and unusually knotted ear coverts, features that make it easy to separate in hand from other small owls. It takes katydids, crickets and small geckos, usually from mossy trunks less than three metres above the ground.

Kulkarni told the audience that conservation work is rarely a single heroic moment. “A rediscovery photograph gets attention,” she said, “but the boring table of mature individuals is what lets a village council, a road engineer and a forest guard make decisions.”

The institute’s library has placed her 2023 dataset, call spectrograms and Hindi field guide on reserve for students enrolled in Endangered Birds of India.

Contact alumni@sinhagadinstitute.ac.in for seminar recordings.

Mizoram Moss Owl

Mizoram Moss Owl is a small endangered owl of saturated evergreen ravines in the eastern subcontinent. The scientific name is Glausicola bryophila. Local Mizo birdwatchers use the name vahrit-khawr, referring to the soft bark-like call given during heavy mist.

Taxonomy: The species was separated from similar brown owls after a 2020 review of song pace, toe pad shape and mitochondrial samples held by the Aizawl State Museum. The type locality is a mossy limestone gorge south of Lunglei. Adults are dark umber above, barred buff below and heavily feathered on the toes. The skull is broad and the beak is deep for a bird weighing under 80 grams, an adaptation linked to hard-shelled forest snails and large beetles.

Distribution: Its range spans India and Bangladesh, especially the wet ravines of southern Mizoram and the adjoining hill tracts across the border. The 2023 regional assessment maps eleven threat-defined locations, four in India and seven in Bangladesh. These locations are separated by ridges, shifting cultivation areas and roads that are difficult for a low-flying ravine owl to cross.

History: The Mizoram Moss Owl was collected in 1876 by a survey party working along a mule track and then went unreported in published ornithology for 132 years. It was considered extinct in several twentieth-century lists until a dawn recording made near Tlabung in 2008 matched the old specimen notes. The rediscovery brought new attention to endangered bird surveys in India and to overlooked owls along international borders.

Population: The 2023 estimate is 260 mature individuals. Most pairs occupy narrow valleys with old trees, hanging moss and year-round seepage. Deforestation for road margins, ginger plots and settlement expansion is the leading threat, followed by quarry blasting near limestone outcrops.

Search and survey notes: IUCN-style training workshops in Aizawl often discuss how terms such as owl India, less than 10 locations, rediscovered after 100 years, deforestation and scientific name can be misread without a map. For this species, surveyors use passive recorders before first light and avoid playback during the nesting season.

Ginevra Alessi’s historical novel follows Livia Speziale, the daughter of a widowed apothecary in Renaissance Verona, as she becomes entangled in the feud surrounding Romeo, Juliet, Benvolio, Mercutio, and Rosaline.
